content: If glucose testing is unavailable and hypoglycemia is suspected, treat the patient empirically and monitor their response. If glucose levels are confirmed to be low, administer 5 mL/kg of D10 (or 1 mL/kg of D50) to children. For adolescents or adults, provide 125–250 mL of D10 rapidly (or 25–50 mL of D50). Use D5 in all maintenance fluids. For further details, refer to the IMAI DCM Quick Check (page 42) or the Child Pocketbook (page 16). For anxiety, provide psychological support as outlined in Section 6. In cases of confusion in cooperative patients, calmly reason with the patient in a non-aggressive manner. Keep the lights on at night to reduce disorientation. Administer 5 mg intramuscularly (adjusted for the patient’s size) if necessary. Approach the patient cautiously, call for assistance, and only provide treatment if it is safe to do so. Additional guidance can be found in the IMAI DCM Quick Check (page 60). For unexplained neurological symptoms, consider thiamine deficiency (beriberi) and administer 50 mg of vitamin B1 intramuscularly or intravenously daily for several days. In managing mild to moderate cases of Ebola, recognize that early symptoms such as fever, headache, and fatigue may not always indicate severe illness. Patients may still be ambulatory, eating, drinking, and not experiencing significant vomiting or diarrhea. All patients should be given oral rehydration solution (ORS) and encouraged to drink it. Monitor patients every shift to detect progression to severe illness. If the patient remains stable, no further laboratory tests are needed after the initial malaria rapid diagnostic test (RDT). For fluid resuscitation, optimize oral and intravenous fluid intake. Actively encourage patients to take frequent sips of ORS. In confirmed wards, mildly ill patients can assist more severely ill patients with ORS intake. If nausea or vomiting occurs, consider administering an antiemetic such as ondansetron. Offer flavored ORS, coconut water, or mix ORS with fruit juice to improve palatability. Provide containers that are easy for patients to handle while lying in bed, such as those with straws or sippy mugs. For children, especially those under two years of age, use a nasogastric (NG) tube if fluid intake is insufficient. Liquid feeds (e.g., F-75) can also be administered via NG tube. Before feeding, confirm NG tube placement by aspirating or flushing with 10 mL of normal saline without causing the child to cough. Assess whether the patient can rely on ORS for hydration or requires IV fluids. Evaluate the patient’s ability to lift the container, the amount of fluid consumed, their ability to get out of bed, and the presence of vomiting, diarrhea, or signs of shock and dehydration. If the patient is very weak, not eating or drinking well, or unconscious, consider starting IV fluids. Maintain a low threshold for initiating IV hydration. For maintenance fluids, calculate the hourly and 24-hour fluid requirements based on body weight. Use the formula: 4 mL/kg/hr for the first 10 kg of body weight, 2 mL/kg/hr for the next 10 kg, and 1 mL/kg/hr for each additional kilogram. Use adult IV giving sets (20 drops = 1 mL) or pediatric burettes (60 drops = 1 mL) as appropriate. If available, use an electronic infusion pump for accurate fluid administration, especially in children. Monitor fluid output and adjust fluid administration accordingly. Watch for signs of overhydration, such as respiratory distress (pulmonary edema) or peripheral edema (swollen feet). Swollen feet alone should not prompt discontinuation of fluids but should lead to careful reassessment for pulmonary edema. Gather all necessary equipment, including sharps containers, adhesive dressings, IV catheters, disinfectant swabs, and tourniquets. Use single-use IV catheter preparation kits and safety catheters with shielded retractable needles when possible. Consider early intraosseous access in patients with difficult IV access, especially in children, using a powered device if available. Monitor IV sites closely for signs of infection or complications. Ribavirin is not effective for Ebola or Marburg disease. Its efficacy in Lassa fever and CCHF is based on observational data, with the best outcomes seen when administered within the first six days of illness. Ribavirin dosing should be adjusted for renal insufficiency. Monitor for side effects, including hemolytic anemia, which is dose-dependent and reversible upon cessation of treatment. Ribavirin is contraindicated in severe anemia, coronary artery disease, renal insufficiency, decompensated liver disease, breastfeeding, and known hypersensitivity. In pregnant women with Ebola, assess the risk of transmission and document pregnancy status in clinical records. Pregnant women with active Ebola or those who survive without pregnancy loss may transmit the virus during delivery or obstetric procedures. Ebola in pregnancy is associated with high rates of obstetric complications and poor maternal and perinatal outcomes, including spontaneous abortion, preterm labor, hemorrhage, and stillbirth. Pregnant women with suspected or confirmed Ebola should be managed in an Ebola treatment unit (ETU) with the capacity for childbirth and obstetric care. Provide uterotonic drugs immediately after delivery to prevent postpartum hemorrhage (PPH). If oxytocin is unavailable, use misoprostol as an alternative. Use misoprostol for medical management. If uterine size corresponds to a gestational age of 13 weeks or less, administer a single dose of 400 micrograms sublingually. For larger uterine sizes, repeat doses every 3–4 hours as needed. If bleeding is excessive, provide IV fluids or blood transfusion and consider manual vacuum aspiration with appropriate safety precautions. Post-abortion care should include contraceptive counseling and provision of post-abortion contraception before discharge.
